```{r setup}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
# Quarto's R process may start without a UTF-8 locale; without one, the minus
# signs in tables and chart labels print as "<U+2212>".
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))

for (f in list.files("../R", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)

# The scenario used throughout: American roulette, always betting red,
# $5 base bet, $400 bankroll.
p <- P_AMERICAN
unit <- 5
bankroll <- 400
edge <- 1 - 2 * p  # house edge on an even-money bet, 2/38

# Formatting helpers for numbers quoted in the text
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
usd <- function(x) scales::dollar(round(x), style_negative = "minus")
cost <- function(x) usd(abs(x))  # a loss written as a positive amount
num <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")

# Chart styling. Charts are drawn small with large text so they stay readable
# when scaled down to phone width: one image has to work at 320px and 680px.
col_mart <- "#2a78d6"   # Martingale
col_bold <- "#eb6834"   # bold play
col_other <- "#8a8f98"  # every other strategy (context, labeled directly)
ink <- CHART_INK
muted <- CHART_MUTED
text_size <- 4.2        # geom_text size, in mm, to match the axis text
theme_set(theme_report())
strategy_colors <- c("Martingale" = col_mart, "Bold play" = col_bold,
                     "Flat bets" = col_other, "Reverse Martingale" = col_other,
                     "D'Alembert" = col_other, "Fibonacci" = col_other)

set.seed(2024)
```

```{r compute}
#| echo: false
# 1. Exact answers for each strategy trying to turn $400 into $800
exact <- compare_exact(all_strategies(), bankroll, p, unit, goal = 2 * bankroll)

# 2. The same question by simulation, 10,000 players per strategy
n_sim <- 10000
sims <- lapply(all_strategies(), function(s) {
  simulate_many(n_sim, s, bankroll, p, unit, goal = 2 * bankroll)
})
sim_summary <- data.frame(
  strategy = sapply(all_strategies(), `[[`, "name"),
  sim_p_goal = sapply(sims, function(d) mean(d$reached_goal)),
  sim_result = sapply(sims, function(d) mean(d$result))
)
both <- merge(exact, sim_summary, by = "strategy")

# 3. The original experiment: Martingale players who never walk away
broke <- simulate_many(n_sim, martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, goal = Inf)
share_ahead <- mean(broke$peak > bankroll)
median_peak <- median(broke$peak)
median_spins <- median(broke$spins)

m <- exact[exact$strategy == "Martingale", ]
b <- exact[exact$strategy == "Bold play", ]
f <- exact[exact$strategy == "Flat bets", ]
r <- exact[exact$strategy == "Reverse Martingale", ]

# 4. Reverse Martingale can overshoot the goal. Average final cash equals
# P(goal) x average cash among winners, because every other session ends at $0.
reverse_avg_winner <- (bankroll + r$exp_result) / r$p_goal

# 5. A $25 target: how often the Martingale wins, and the two possible results
m25 <- solve_exact(martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, bankroll + 25)

# 6. What a $100 table maximum does to the $400 -> $800 comparison
b100 <- solve_exact(bold_play(), bankroll, p, unit, 2 * bankroll, table_max = 100)
m100 <- solve_exact(martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, 2 * bankroll, table_max = 100)

# 7. Losing-streak odds quoted in the text
streak_at <- function(n) prob_losing_streak(7, n, 1 - p)
# 8. The Martingale players from step 2, followed over time
mart_sims <- sims$martingale
first_win <- min(mart_sims$spins[mart_sims$reached_goal])
broke_by_first_win <- mean(mart_sims$spins <= first_win & !mart_sims$reached_goal)
status_end <- ceiling(quantile(mart_sims$spins, 0.99))

# 9. Chart alt text and captions that quote computed numbers
alt_run <- sprintf("Heat map of cash over spins for 2,000 simulated Martingale players starting at $400. A dark ridge climbs steadily, with fainter bands below it. A typical player climbs to about %s, then falls to zero.", usd(median_peak))
alt_bet <- sprintf("Bar chart of the average total amount bet per session. Bold play bets $400 and loses %s. The Martingale bets %s and loses %s. Flat bets bet the most, %s, and lose almost the whole $400.", cost(b$exp_result), usd(m$exp_wagered), cost(m$exp_result), usd(f$exp_wagered))
alt_streak <- sprintf("Line chart rising with spins played. The chance of at least one streak of seven losses reaches %s by spin 120 and %s by spin 500.", pct(streak_at(120), 0), pct(streak_at(500), 0))
alt_compare <- sprintf("Bar chart of the chance of doubling $400. Bold play %s, Martingale %s, Reverse Martingale %s, Fibonacci %s, D'Alembert %s, flat bets %s. Simulated results sit close to each exact value.",
                       pct(b$p_goal), pct(m$p_goal), pct(r$p_goal), pct(exact$p_goal[exact$strategy == "Fibonacci"]),
                       pct(exact$p_goal[exact$strategy == "D'Alembert"]), pct(f$p_goal, 2))
alt_tail <- sprintf("Two blocks on a shared zero line. A wide, shallow block shows %s of sessions winning $25. A narrow, deep block shows %s of sessions losing $400.", pct(m25$p_goal), pct(1 - m25$p_goal))
alt_status <- sprintf("Stacked area chart of all players over time. Nearly everyone starts out playing. The went-broke area grows steadily from the first spins, and the reached-target area only appears around spin %s, ending near %s.", num(first_win), pct(m$p_goal, 0))
cap_status <- sprintf("Every simulated player's state after each spin. The chart ends at spin %s, by which time 99%% of sessions were over.", num(status_end))
cap_tail <- sprintf("Each block's area is its contribution to the average result: +%s from wins and −%s from losses, which nets to %s per session.",
                    usd(m25$p_goal * 25), usd((1 - m25$p_goal) * bankroll), usd(m25$exp_result))
```

::: findings
**What this project finds** (American roulette, betting red, $400 bankroll, trying to reach $800)

1. **A betting system can't change the house edge.** Your average loss is the edge
   (`r pct(edge, 2)`) times the total amount you bet. That is a known result, and the
   exact calculations here confirm it for all six strategies. What the Martingale changes
   is how much you bet: `r usd(m$exp_wagered)` on average to chase a $400 profit.
2. **A single bold bet beats the Martingale.** One $400 bet on red doubles your money
   `r pct(b$p_goal)` of the time and costs `r cost(b$exp_result)` on average. The
   Martingale succeeds `r pct(m$p_goal)` of the time and costs `r cost(m$exp_result)`.
3. **A high win rate is the wrong thing to measure.** Aim for a small profit and the
   Martingale wins most sessions, yet it still loses money on average. That pattern
   of frequent small gains and rare ruinous losses shows up well beyond the casino.
:::

## The promise

In the carnival of 1754, Giacomo Casanova was gambling in Venice with money
belonging to his lover. His memoirs record that, "playing the martingale, and
doubling my stakes continuously, I won every day during the remainder of the
carnival." Not long after, the story ends the way it usually does: "I still
played on the martingale, but with such bad luck that I was soon left without a
sequin." [@casanova]

The system is simple. Bet one unit on red. If you lose, double the bet. When you
finally win, that one win recovers every loss in the streak plus one unit of profit,
and you start again. Since red has to come up eventually, it *feels* like a machine
for printing small, steady wins.

```{r single-run}
#| fig-cap: "Where the money is. Shading shows how many of 2,000 Martingale players who never walk away held each amount at each spin, darker meaning more. Players drop out of the picture as they go broke. The black line is the player closest to the median on peak and session length. The view stops at 400 spins and $1,500."
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_run
set.seed(11)
runs <- lapply(1:2000, function(i) simulate_player(martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, path = TRUE))

plot_session_density(session_density(runs, max_spin = 400, max_cash = 1500), bankroll,
                     typical = typical_run(runs), text_size = text_size) +
  labs(title = "Most players climb, then fall off a cliff",
       subtitle = "$5 base bet, $400 bankroll, American roulette")
```

The dark ridge is the promise: a steady climb of $5 at a time. The fainter bands below it are players recovering from a big hit. Among `r num(n_sim)` simulated players who use
the Martingale and never walk away, **`r pct(share_ahead)` were ahead of their starting
$400 at some point**. The median player's best moment was `r usd(median_peak)`, and the
median session lasted `r num(median_spins)` spins. In the end every one of them lost
the whole bankroll, but that isn't a finding: a player who never stops in a game with a
house edge will always go broke eventually. The useful question is what happens to
players who *do* plan to stop.

## Why no system can win

Here is the rule that settles it. On every spin, a bet on red loses `r pct(edge, 2)`
of its stake on average. A betting system decides *how much* to stake and *when to
stop*, but it can't change the edge on any single spin. So over a whole session:

::: formula
average result = −house edge × average total amount bet
:::

This is Wald's identity applied to gambling, so it is true by mathematics rather than
something this project discovered. Pflaumer [-@pflaumer] points to Ethier's proof that
it holds for every betting system [@ethier, p. 298] and to Epstein's summary that all
betting systems "lead ultimately to the same mathematical expectation of gain per unit
amount wagered" [@epstein, p. 52].

That makes it a useful test of this project's code. The exact solver works out each
strategy's average result from its final bankrolls, without using the house edge, and
its loss still comes out at `r pct(edge, 2)` of the amount bet every time, as the table
below shows. What differs between strategies is how much they bet:

```{r total-bet}
#| fig-cap: "Exact results for six strategies, each trying to turn $400 into $800."
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_bet
bets <- exact |>
  arrange(desc(exp_wagered)) |>
  mutate(strategy = factor(strategy, levels = strategy),
         label = paste0(usd(exp_wagered), " bet, ", cost(exp_result), " lost"))

ggplot(bets, aes(exp_wagered, strategy)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = exp_wagered, yend = strategy, color = strategy),
               linewidth = 2.4, lineend = "round") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 180, size = text_size - 0.4, color = ink) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 13500), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "You lose in proportion to what you bet",
       subtitle = "Average total bet per session, and 5.26% of it lost") +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

```{r identity-table}
#| echo: false
exact |>
  arrange(desc(p_goal)) |>
  transmute(Strategy = strategy,
            `Average total bet` = usd(exp_wagered),
            `Average result` = usd(exp_result),
            `Result ÷ amount bet` = paste0("−", pct(abs(exp_result / exp_wagered), 2)),
            `Average spins` = num(exp_spins)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The word *martingale* has a second life here. In 1939 the French mathematician
Jean Ville borrowed the gamblers' term for a new idea in probability theory: a fair
game in which, whatever you know so far, your expected future fortune equals your
present one [@mansuy]. Joseph Doob developed the idea into one of the central tools of
modern probability. A central result, the *optional stopping theorem*, says that
with finite money and finite time, no rule for sizing bets or choosing when to stop can
turn a fair game into a favorable one, let alone an unfavorable game like roulette. The
system gave the mathematics its name, and the mathematics shows why the system can't work.

## Why it feels like it works anyway

The Martingale's appeal is real. It wins small amounts most of the time, and it fails
only when a losing streak runs longer than the bankroll can cover.

With a $5 base bet, a $400 bankroll covers
`r max_covered_streak(bankroll, unit)` losses in a row
($5 + $10 + … + $160 = $315). The seventh bet would be $320 with only $85 left.
Seven straight losses have a probability of
`r pct((1 - p)^7, 2)` from any given starting point, which feels safe. Over a long
session it stops being safe:

```{r streak}
#| fig-cap: "Exact probability, from the run-length formula in R/formulas.R."
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_streak
spins <- 1:600
streak_df <- data.frame(spins = spins, prob = sapply(spins, streak_at))
marks <- streak_df[streak_df$spins %in% c(120, 500), ]
marks$label <- paste0(pct(marks$prob, 0), " by spin ", marks$spins)

ggplot(streak_df, aes(spins, prob)) +
  geom_line(color = col_mart, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = marks, color = col_mart, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = label), hjust = c(-0.12, 0.9), vjust = c(1.3, 3.4),
            size = text_size, color = ink) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Spins played", y = "Chance of a 7-loss streak",
       title = "Rare at any moment, likely in a long session",
       subtitle = "At least 7 straight losses betting red, American roulette")
```

This is a simplified picture, because a player's bankroll moves. Someone who has built
it up to $635 can cover seven losses, and the fatal streak becomes eight.

Can a bigger bankroll fix this? Each extra loss you want to cover **doubles** the money
you need, but only cuts the chance of the fatal streak by a factor of
`r round(1 - p, 3)`. Meanwhile the average loss stays the same share of everything you
bet. Casinos also set table maximums, which stop the doubling at a fixed point no matter
how rich the player is [@pflaumer]. The simulator models this: when the next doubled bet
would exceed the limit, the player takes the loss and starts again at the base bet.

```{r bankroll-table}
#| echo: false
streaks <- 4:12
chance <- sapply(streaks + 1, function(k) prob_losing_streak(k, 500, 1 - p))
tibble(`Losses covered` = streaks,
       `Bankroll needed` = usd(unit * (2^streaks - 1)),
       `Chance of a longer streak within 500 spins` = ifelse(chance > 0.999, ">99.9%", pct(chance))) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "rrr")
```

## If you must gamble

Suppose the goal is modest and concrete: turn $400 into $800, then go home. Which
strategy gives the best chance?

```{r compare}
#| fig-cap: "Bars show exact probabilities. The dot and whisker under each bar show 10,000 simulated players with a 95% interval."
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_compare
cmp <- both |>
  arrange(p_goal) |>
  mutate(strategy = factor(strategy, levels = strategy),
         row = as.numeric(strategy),
         se = sqrt(sim_p_goal * (1 - sim_p_goal) / n_sim),
         label = ifelse(p_goal < 0.01, pct(p_goal, 2), pct(p_goal)))

ggplot(cmp, aes(y = row)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = p_goal, yend = row, color = strategy),
               linewidth = 2.4, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = p_goal, color = strategy), size = 2.6) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = sim_p_goal - 1.96 * se, xmax = sim_p_goal + 1.96 * se, y = row - 0.28),
                 color = ink, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = sim_p_goal, y = row - 0.28), color = ink, size = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = p_goal, label = label), hjust = -0.3, size = text_size, color = ink) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = cmp$row, labels = as.character(cmp$strategy)) +
  labs(x = "Chance of doubling $400", y = NULL,
       title = "One big bet beats every progression",
       subtitle = "Exact answers, checked against simulation") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r compare-table}
#| echo: false
both |>
  arrange(desc(p_goal)) |>
  transmute(Strategy = strategy,
            `Chance of doubling (exact)` = pct(p_goal, 2),
            `Simulated (10,000 players)` = pct(sim_p_goal, 2),
            `Average result (exact)` = usd(exp_result),
            `Simulated average` = usd(sim_result)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The winner is **bold play**: bet whatever gets you to the goal in one win, or everything
you have if that's less. Here that means a single $400 bet on red. It succeeds with
probability exactly 18/38 = `r pct(b$p_goal)` and costs `r cost(b$exp_result)` on average,
because you only expose $400 to the house edge once.

This isn't a quirk of the scenario. Dubins and Savage proved in *How to Gamble If You
Must* that in a game where the odds are against you, bold play maximizes the chance of
reaching a fixed goal [@dubins-savage]. The identity above gives the intuition. When a
session can only end broke or exactly at the goal (true for flat bets, the Martingale
and bold play), the average final bankroll is simply the goal times the chance of
reaching it. Combining that with the identity gives:

::: formula
chance of reaching the goal = (bankroll − house edge × average total amount bet) ÷ goal
:::

For the Martingale: ($400 − 5.26% × `r usd(m$exp_wagered)`) ÷ $800 = `r pct(m$p_goal)`.
Among these strategies, every extra dollar bet costs the same slice of the chance of
getting there, so betting less means reaching the goal more often. Flat $5 bets are the
extreme case. They need about `r num(f$exp_spins)` spins on average, and the edge grinds
the chance of doubling down to `r pct(f$p_goal, 2)`.

The reverse Martingale shows where that formula stops applying. It bets slightly less
than the Martingale, yet reaches the goal less often, because its winning streaks can
overshoot. Its successful players finish with `r usd(reverse_avg_winner)` on average,
not $800, so the same average bankroll is spread across fewer, larger wins.

In practice, bold play needs a table that accepts the bet. At a $100 table maximum, its
chance of doubling falls to `r pct(b100$p_goal)`, though that is still well above the
Martingale's `r pct(m100$p_goal)` at the same table.

Following the Martingale players over time shows how those odds play out. The first
of the `r num(n_sim)` simulated players reached $800 on spin `r num(first_win)`, and by
then `r pct(broke_by_first_win, 0)` had already gone broke:

```{r status}
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_status
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_status
plot_status(status_over_time(mart_sims$spins, mart_sims$reached_goal, status_end)) +
  labs(title = "Nearly half go broke before anyone wins",
       subtitle = "10,000 Martingale players trying to turn $400 into $800")
```

None of this makes roulette a good investment. Every strategy in the table has a negative
average. Bold play is simply the least bad way to chase a fixed target.

## A high win rate is the wrong metric

The Martingale's real appeal is its win rate. Aim for a small enough profit and it
"works" most of the time. A player with $400 who walks away after winning $25 succeeds
**`r pct(m25$p_goal)`** of the time. The other `r pct(1 - m25$p_goal)` of sessions lose
the whole $400:

```{r tail}
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_tail
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_tail
w <- m25$p_goal
blocks <- data.frame(xmin = c(0, w), xmax = c(w, 1), ymin = c(0, -bankroll), ymax = c(25, 0))

ggplot(blocks) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = col_mart) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = muted, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = w / 2, y = 95, label = paste0("Win $25\n", pct(w), " of sessions"),
           size = text_size, color = ink, lineheight = 0.95) +
  annotate("text", x = w - 0.03, y = -bankroll / 2, hjust = 1,
           label = paste0("Lose $400\n", pct(1 - w), " of sessions"),
           size = text_size, color = ink, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) scales::dollar(x, style_negative = "minus"),
                     limits = c(-bankroll, 150), breaks = c(-400, -200, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Share of sessions", y = "Result",
       title = "Usually win a little, sometimes lose it all",
       subtitle = "Martingale, $400 bankroll, walking away at +$25")
```

The average result is still `r usd(m25$exp_result)`. Someone who judged the strategy by
its win rate, or by a short run of sessions, would think it was excellent. The same
holds across targets:

```{r win-rate}
#| fig-cap: "Exact results for a $400 bankroll. Bold play's line is bumpy because the number of bets it needs depends on how the target relates to the bankroll."
#| fig-height: 6.4
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked line charts for profit targets from $25 to $400. The chance of hitting the target falls from about 90% to 47% for bold play and 35% for the Martingale. The average result is negative everywhere, reaching about minus $117 for the Martingale and staying near minus $20 for bold play."
targets <- seq(25, 400, by = 25)
wr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(targets, function(t) {
  rbind(
    cbind(target = t, strategy = "Martingale",
          as.data.frame(solve_exact(martingale(), bankroll, p, unit, bankroll + t)[c("p_goal", "exp_result")])),
    cbind(target = t, strategy = "Bold play",
          as.data.frame(solve_exact(bold_play(), bankroll, p, unit, bankroll + t)[c("p_goal", "exp_result")]))
  )
}))

# Label each line at its right end: bold play above its line, Martingale below.
end_labels <- wr |> filter(target == max(targets)) |>
  mutate(vjust = ifelse(strategy == "Bold play", -0.8, 1.8))
g1 <- ggplot(wr, aes(target, p_goal, color = strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = end_labels, aes(label = strategy, vjust = vjust), hjust = 1,
            size = text_size - 0.4, color = ink) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Chance of hitting the target", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left",
        legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), legend.box.spacing = unit(2, "pt"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "plain", size = rel(1)))
g2 <- ggplot(wr, aes(target, exp_result, color = strategy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = muted, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = end_labels, aes(label = strategy, vjust = vjust), hjust = 1,
            size = text_size - 0.4, color = ink) +
  scale_color_manual(values = strategy_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) scales::dollar(x, style_negative = "minus")) +
  expand_limits(y = -140) +  # room for the Martingale label under its line
  labs(x = "Profit target", y = NULL, title = "Average result") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "plain", size = rel(1)))
g1 / g2 + plot_annotation(
  title = "Win often, still lose on average",
  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.1)))
)
```

That payoff shape (usually win a little, occasionally lose almost everything) is not
unique to roulette. The examples below are **analogies, not claims that markets are
roulette wheels**. What they share is the shape of the payoff, not the odds.

- **Doubling down at Barings.** Brown and Steenbeek studied exchange data from Nick
  Leeson's trading in Singapore and found that he "continuously doubled his position
  as prices were falling". The losses, around US$1.4 billion, brought down Barings
  Bank in 1995 [@brown-steenbeek]. Their warning applies to any doubler: the eventual
  loss "is preceded by a period of high returns with low volatility", which looks
  like skill until it isn't.
- **Betting on calm markets.** Short-volatility exchange-traded products profit
  steadily while stock markets stay calm. On February 5, 2018, a jump in volatility
  caused a one-day loss of more than 90% in their value [@augustin-volmageddon].
- **"Martingale" trading bots.** Automated strategies that add to a losing position at
  set intervals are commissioned for retail forex platforms such as MetaTrader under
  that name [@mql5-grid]. They follow the same logic as the roulette system, and they
  carry the same risk.

The lesson for anyone evaluating a strategy, model or product metric: **a success rate
says nothing about the size of the failures.** Look at the expected value and the tail of
the distribution, and be wary of any evaluation window that may simply not have been long
enough to catch the rare bad outcome.

## Try it yourself

Pick a strategy, bankroll, target and table limit below to see the exact odds, with
simulated players as a check. It updates as you type, and you can hover over the charts
for exact values. The explorer runs on a small JavaScript copy of the R engine, and every
build checks the two against each other.

::: column-page
<iframe id="explorer-frame" class="explorer-frame" src="explorer/index.html" title="Betting strategy explorer"></iframe>
:::

```{=html}
<script>
  // Size the embed to its content, so it never needs its own scrollbar. The explorer
  // reports height changes, but its first report can arrive before this script runs,
  // so also measure once it has loaded.
  (function () {
    var frame = document.getElementById("explorer-frame");
    function measure() {
      var doc = frame.contentDocument;
      if (doc && doc.body && doc.body.offsetHeight) frame.style.height = doc.body.offsetHeight + "px";
    }
    window.addEventListener("message", function (event) {
      if (event.origin === window.location.origin && event.data && event.data.explorerHeight) {
        frame.style.height = event.data.explorerHeight + "px";
      }
    });
    frame.addEventListener("load", measure);
    measure();
  })();
</script>
```

## How the numbers were produced

Every result comes from two independent engines that share the same strategy
definitions (`R/strategies.R`):

- **Simulation** (`R/simulate.R`): plays each session spin by spin with random outcomes.
- **Exact solver** (`R/exact.R`): with a fixed goal, a session is a Markov chain whose state
  is (cash in hand, the strategy's memory, such as the current bet). The solver lists
  every reachable state and solves the chain's linear equations for the probability of
  reaching the goal, the expected amount bet, the expected number of spins and the
  expected final bankroll. No random numbers are involved.

The test suite (`tests/testthat/`) checks the two engines against each other and against
published results:

| Check | Compared against |
|---|---|
| Flat betting | The classical gambler's-ruin formula |
| Bold play | The Dubins–Savage recursion |
| Every strategy, two wheels, with and without table limits | Average result = −edge × amount bet |
| Every strategy in a fair game | Average result of exactly zero |
| Martingale round statistics with a table limit | Pflaumer (2019), Table 1 |
| Losing-streak probabilities | Brute-force enumeration of all 1,024 ten-spin sequences |
| Simulation vs exact solver, all six strategies | Agreement within four standard errors |
| The explorer's JavaScript engine, in 36 settings | The R exact solver |

The code for each chart is folded beneath it. The setup code and tables are in the
[report source](https://github.com/RustyRockets/martingale-simulator/blob/main/report/index.qmd).

## Assumptions and limits

- The wheel is fair and spins are independent. Every bet is on an even-money chance
  (red/black), with no *la partage* or *en prison* rules. Those rules halve the house
  edge on European wheels and would shrink every loss in this report, but they don't
  change the conclusions.
- Bets come in whole $5 units and must be at least the base bet, except that a player
  who can't cover the next bet stakes everything they have left. There is no table
  limit unless stated.
- The headline scenario ($400 bankroll, $800 goal) is one choice among many. Bold play's
  first place is a theorem, for any bankroll and goal without a table limit. The order of
  the other strategies changes with the scenario, and so do the exact percentages. The
  explorer lets you try others.
- The finance examples illustrate a payoff shape. They are not a model of any market.
